name: Codivilla method

lead: The Codivilla method is the name given to the limb-lengthening operation that Italian orthopaedic surgeon Alessandro Codivilla published in 1905. The femur was cut, a pin was placed through the heel bone, and a strong pulling force was applied so the two bone ends separated and the leg ended up longer.

For people interested in height, it matters as the starting point of the idea that bone can be made longer by surgery. Modern cosmetic leg lengthening uses motorised nails or external frames rather than Codivilla's heel traction, but historians of the field describe the principles and complications of today's techniques as traceable to his work.

paras: Historically it was a hospital procedure for people with short or deformed legs, not a self-directed practice. The femur was divided, traction through a calcaneal (heel) pin pulled the segments apart, and the limb was then held in a cast while bone healed. Today it is not used for height; surgeons use gradual-distraction devices such as the Ilizarov frame or internal lengthening nails.

Codivilla's own series is reported to have had many complications, including infection, tissue death and failure of the bone to heal, and his approach was not widely adopted. Modern lengthening, which descends from the same principles, still carries risks such as infection, bone healing problems, hardware failure and nerve injury, and is performed only by specialist surgeons.

angle.text: The method showed that a leg bone could be lengthened by surgery, which is the principle behind today's cosmetic height-lengthening operations. In its original form it was a hospital treatment for short or deformed legs, and modern patients seeking height are treated with later techniques.

lead: The Codivilla method is the early twentieth-century limb-lengthening technique described by the Italian surgeon Alessandro Codivilla (1861-1912), director of the Rizzoli Orthopaedic Institute in Bologna. In 1905 he published an account of lengthening the lower limb by cutting the femur and applying heavy traction through a pin placed in the heel bone (calcaneus).[1][2]

It is relevant to height-focused communities because it is the first documented clinical attempt to make a person's leg bone longer. A historical review of limb lengthening states that the principles and complications of the three major later advances, Ilizarov circular fixators, computer-assisted six-strut frames and motorised intramedullary nails, rest on observations made by Codivilla, Putti and Abbott roughly 110 years ago.[3] Today's cosmetic leg lengthening, in which people seek added height through surgery, belongs to that lineage.

Codivilla's operation itself was devised for patients with short or malformed limbs. According to an overview of limb lengthening, he treated 26 patients, and his report described many complications including infection, tissue death and failed bone union, so the method was not adopted widely.[4] It was later superseded by the gradual-distraction approach developed by Gavriil Ilizarov from the 1950s.[4]

paras: Codivilla's lengthening procedure involved dividing the thigh bone and then pulling the two segments apart using traction applied through a pin driven through the heel bone. The 1905 paper on the means of lengthening the lower limbs appeared in the American Journal of Orthopedic Surgery, and Codivilla followed it with a 1910 paper on indications and technique of extension with a nail.[5] He is credited with early development of skeletal traction, in which force is applied directly to bone through a pin rather than through the skin.[5]
The overview of limb lengthening gives the 1905 series as 26 people born with malformed legs and notes that its reported complications were extensive.[4]

sections.h: The surgeon and the Bologna school
paras: Codivilla was born in Bologna in 1861, graduated in medicine in 1886, served as chief surgeon at Imola and was invited in 1899 to direct the Rizzoli Institute, where he moved his focus from general surgery to orthopaedics. He resigned the directorship in 1908 and died in 1912; Vittorio Putti succeeded him at Rizzoli.[5] A history of the Bolognese orthopaedic school credits Rizzoli, Codivilla and Putti with the Institute's international recognition.[1]

Codivilla's name is also attached to other procedures, including a posteromedial release for clubfoot, a capsular arthroplasty for hip dislocation and an early pancreatic head resection, which are separate from his lengthening work.[6][7]

Von Langenbeck proposed bone lengthening in 1869, and Codivilla's 1905 report was the first clinical attempt described in the literature.[4] A review of limb lengthening lists Codivilla, Putti and Abbott as the pioneers whose observations underlie later techniques.[3] The same review identifies three major advances of recent decades, the Ilizarov method, computer-assisted circular fixators and motorised lengthening nails.[3]

Ilizarov, a Russian surgeon working from the 1950s, identified a rate of gradual separation that allowed bone to regenerate, which led to wide adoption.[4] Cosmetic lengthening has since grown in demand in places such as India, where it is reported to be largely unregulated, and China's health ministry banned the operation in 2006 after serious side effects.[4]

Codivilla's series is described as having produced infection, tissue death and non-union.[4] In modern gradual lengthening, published approximate rates include infection of about 5 percent, bone healing in the wrong alignment of 7 to 9 percent and hardware failure of 3 to 4.5 percent; separating the bone too fast can cause non-union and too slowly can allow premature union.[4]
No studies found on the Codivilla method as a current treatment. Historical and review literature describes it as the origin of later techniques.[3][8]
